morningLine: This week: Commodore 64 shelf talk grows louder, the IBM PC afterglow keeps compatibility on buyers' minds, E.T. returns to the top of the weekend box office, The Beastmaster opens, and Billy Squier rules album-rock radio.

lead.headline: Commodore 64 Moves From Spec Sheet to Store Talk
lead.summary: By mid-August 1982, the Commodore 64 is no longer just a CES promise. The machine's 64K memory headline, color graphics, SID sound chip, cartridge slot, and aggressive home-computer price point give computer stores a fresh answer to Atari, Apple, TI, and IBM conversations. The real story is not one launch-day ribbon cutting; it is the moment when the C64 starts becoming a retail question families can actually ask across the counter.
lead.confidence: August 1982 retail-era context; exact-day launch claims avoided

computerItems.label: Home computers
computerItems.headline: Commodore 64 Enters the Retail Conversation
computerItems.summary: Commodore's 64K machine gives stores a new pitch: more memory than many rivals, color graphics, SID sound, and a family-computer price that can sit beside game-machine and schoolwork arguments.

computerItems.label: IBM PC
computerItems.headline: Compatibility Becomes the Real Anniversary Story
computerItems.summary: The IBM PC's first year turns into a compatibility lesson: buyers care less about romance and more about expansion cards, printers, DOS disks, spreadsheets, and whether the whole desk behaves on Monday morning.
computerItems.confidence: One-year IBM PC context carried from August 12 anniversary week

computerItems.label: Peripherals
computerItems.headline: Disk Drives and Printers Eat the Budget
computerItems.summary: Home-computer price tags rarely end at the keyboard. Disk drives, cassette decks, monitors, modems, printers, paper, and blank media turn the real purchase into a desk-sized system.

computerItems.label: Software
computerItems.headline: Type-In Programs Still Matter
computerItems.summary: Magazine listings and user-group code remain part of the weekly software economy, especially for families waiting for commercial C64 and Atari shelves to fill in.

market.headline: Store Desk: The Computer Is Only the First Box
market.summary: The week's retail math is not just C64 versus Atari, Apple, TI, or IBM. It is the stack of add-ons: monitor, storage, printer, paper, joysticks, modem, and named software that make the machine useful.

curiosity.headline: E.T. Takes the Weekend Back
curiosity.summary: The August 20-22 domestic weekend returns E.T. to No. 1, a reminder that the summer's biggest movie still has enough gravity to bend the rest of the culture page around it.

frontPageStories.label: Home Computers

frontPageStories.summary: August 1982 puts the C64 into the practical buyer conversation: 64K, color, sound, cartridges, cassette/disk choices, and a price that made families compare it with Atari, Apple, TI, and PC desks.

frontPageStories.label: IBM PC
frontPageStories.headline: PC Compatibility Still Sells the Desk
frontPageStories.summary: One week after the IBM PC's first birthday, the question remains which boards, printers, DOS disks, and business programs will behave together without making the buyer become the service department.
